forces: Mixed chorus and orchestra with organ
performers: Wiener Staatsopernchor; Wiener Philharmoniker; Franz Sauer, organ; Bruno Walter, conductor
recorded: Live, 26 July 1956, Small Festival Hall, Salzburg
question: What holds the movement together across the change of composing hand?
intro: The opening string figures seem to catch their breath before the choir sings. Mozart’s draft stops after eight bars; Süssmayr carries the movement onwards in the traditional completion. Its power comes from more than that famous break: follow the first ascent, the quieter prayer and the renewed plea that reaches a major-coloured ending.

sections.label: A · Lament and ascent
sections.mNote: Broken string gestures support a gathering choral phrase

sections.label: B · Quieter prayer
sections.mNote: The texture lightens for a more intimate plea

sections.label: A′ · Renewed plea
sections.mNote: The opening gesture regains weight in the concluding prayer

sections.label: Close · Amen
sections.mNote: Moving figures settle into a sustained major-coloured ending

cues.title: A phrase made from broken gestures
cues.text: The opening belongs to the upper strings alone. Their short paired notes are separated by rests, making a wavering surface before the choir joins. Listen for those gaps: the sense of lament is in the interrupted motion as much as the melody.
cues.evidence: NMA p. 111 and Breitkopf p. 49 show two bars for violins and violas before the voices and lower parts. The report’s quiet 0:00–0:10 and rise around 0:15 support the broad opening contrast, not an exact entrance time.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A completion enters print
cues.text: The Requiem’s first published full score appears in 1800, several years after Mozart’s death. The familiar Lacrimosa therefore reaches its early readers as a completed movement, not just the eight bars preserved in Mozart’s unfinished draft.
cues.evidence: Nowak’s NMA preface discusses the 1800 Breitkopf & Härtel publication and the surviving manuscript: https://dme.mozarteum.at/DME/objs/pdf/nma_14_-23_-3_eng.pdf. This publication date belongs to the composition, not this recording.

cues.title: The broken phrase learns to climb
cues.text: In the first ascent, the choir rises from separated syllables towards a stronger, more connected utterance. The small string gestures continue underneath. Follow how the same pulse can support both hesitation and gathering force.
cues.evidence: NMA p. 112, bars 5–8, shows the rising choral line and crescendo. The report rises sharply at 0:40–0:45 after lower levels at 0:25–0:35. This places the ascent broadly, without marking Mozart’s final manuscript bar in the audio.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Beyond the surviving draft
cues.text: Süssmayr’s continuation does not begin a separate movement. It extends the lament using the same rocking metre and characteristic string figures. Listen for continuity across the phrases rather than expecting the change of author to sound like a cut in the recording.
cues.evidence: NMA pp. 111–113 explicitly distinguishes Mozart’s first eight bars from Süssmayr’s continuation. The report’s first crest at 0:45 and withdrawal after 0:48 place this cue beyond the initial ascent. No exact timestamp is assigned to the authorship seam.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Another hand before Süssmayr
cues.text: Constanze first entrusts the unfinished score to Joseph Eybler, who leaves a receipt dated 21 December 1791. His work breaks off in the Lacrimosa. Süssmayr’s later completion is a separate stage in the manuscript’s history, not simply Mozart dictating a finished score.
cues.evidence: Nowak’s NMA preface prints the documentary sequence and discusses Eybler’s two added soprano bars. The note does not identify Eybler’s version with the completion used in this recording.

cues.title: The prayer becomes more intimate
cues.text: The middle prayer is lighter in scoring and lower in pressure than the preceding ascent. Keep following the strings’ small gestures beneath the voices: the movement has withdrawn, but its characteristic pulse has not disappeared.
cues.evidence: NMA p. 114, from Huic ergo, reduces the scoring; Breitkopf p. 52. The report’s 1:32 boundary and lower relative level from 1:30 to 2:10 support this broad quieter span.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The plea regains its weight
cues.text: The later prayer gathers strength again. Familiar rising-and-falling gestures make the renewed sound belong to the opening lament, even though the text has moved from describing tears to asking that the dead be granted rest.
cues.evidence: NMA pp. 115–116 connects the quieter prayer to the renewed dona eis requiem material. The report’s 2:16 boundary and rise at 2:15–2:25 locate the change approximately; the cue does not time an individual word.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Walter does not treat every doubling as fixed
cues.text: Walter is quoted as removing some trombone doublings of the choir to lighten Süssmayr’s orchestration. That documents an interpretative policy, not a list of cuts in this performance. We cannot identify every instrumental omission from the source information alone.
cues.evidence: Nowak’s NMA preface, printed p. XX, note 53, quotes Walter via Henry H. Hausner (1964). No session-specific annotated score is supplied by Commons, Internet Archive or the concert archive; uncertain trombone activity is therefore not plotted.

cues.title: Motion beneath the held plea
cues.text: As the final prayer lengthens, compare the singers’ broader notes with the still-moving strings. A sustained vocal sound can contain considerable motion underneath; the ending has to bring both layers to rest.
cues.evidence: NMA pp. 116–117 shows broadening vocal values over continuing violin figures. The report remains comparatively strong through 2:45–3:10. This is a listening strategy for the closing passage, not a separated-instrument observation.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A short Amen, not a fugue
cues.text: The completion closes with a brief, sustained Amen rather than an extended contrapuntal finale. The final D chord has a major third. Listen to the contrast between that settled sonority and the broken string gestures with which the movement began.
cues.evidence: NMA p. 117, final two bars; Breitkopf p. 54. The final written F♯ supplies the major third. The report shows a strong 3:00–3:10 span and a low tail after about 3:20; it does not establish the exact final chord or release.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The lament thins into a personal plea
transitions.how: After the first ascent and its continuation, the score reduces the orchestral weight for Huic ergo. Winds and brass fall away from the start of this prayer, leaving choir and a lighter string foundation. The interrupted accompaniment remains recognisable, but the vocal line turns towards petition rather than another rising proclamation. The link is made through retained rhythm and reduced scoring, not a sudden new tempo.
transitions.evidence: NMA pp. 113–114, especially the change at bar 15; Breitkopf pp. 51–52. The report’s 1:32 boundary follows a drop in relative level near 1:30. This is an approximate section placement, not a word-aligned entrance.

transitions.title: The opening gesture gathers weight again
transitions.how: The lighter prayer leads into an instrumental preparation and a stronger choral appeal for rest. The opening’s characteristic rising-and-falling figure is recovered in a fuller setting. Winds reinforce the voices again and the lower parts add weight, while the compound pulse continues without a new metre. The return is a reshaping of the lament for the closing words, not a repeat of the whole opening.
transitions.evidence: NMA pp. 115–116, including the instrumental bar before the renewed choral plea; Breitkopf p. 53. The report shows a pronounced rise around 2:15 and a novelty peak at 2:16. The timing is provisional.

transitions.title: The moving prayer settles on Amen
transitions.how: The repeated appeals for rest lead to a short closing Amen. The strings continue their small figures beneath sustained voices before joining the final held sonority. A written F♯ gives the last D chord a major third, changing the colour of a movement rooted in D minor. The completion closes the Sequence here with a brief cadence, not an added Amen fugue.
transitions.evidence: NMA p. 117 and Breitkopf p. 54. The 3:00 report boundary and high final windows at 3:05–3:10 anchor the closing span; no chord is inferred from automatic key estimates. NMA prints a final fermata.

source.title: Mozart–Süssmayr Requiem, Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Dover unabridged reprint
source.locator: Printed pp. 49–54, checked against NMA pp. 111–117. Passage-level states estimated from the report, not exact entrances or continuous activity. Basset horns lack a stage token. Trombones are omitted from this partial map because Walter’s reported cuts have no session-specific documentation.

timeline.note: The opening two bars contain only upper strings; short figures and rests establish the interrupted pulse.
The first choral phrase adds low support and reed colour to the continuing upper-string gestures.
Across the first ascent, the voices rise and brass and timpani punctuate its crest; this is not a claim of continuous tutti playing.
The quieter prayer begins with choir and lighter strings; winds and brass rest at this change in the score.
The renewed plea restores fuller support around the familiar rising-and-falling figure; brass and drums punctuate the span.
The closing Amen lengthens the vocal notes while the strings finish their moving figures and settle into the last chord.
The report reaches its low final tail. No further scored activity is assigned.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Wiener Staatsopernchor (chorus), Wiener Philharmoniker (orchestra), Franz Sauer (organ), Bruno Walter (conductor)
fields.note: This movement is for chorus, without a solo vocal part; the concert’s vocal solo quartet is not credited as singing here. Commons and Internet Archive name the Wiener Staatsopernchor; the festival catalogue uses Konzertvereinigung Wiener Staatsopernchor. The primary concert archive confirms Walter, the orchestra, all four concert soloists and Franz Sauer, but leaves its choir field blank. Ira Malaniuk, Anton Dermota and Cesare Siepi belong to the full concert cast, not to an invented solo entrance in this movement.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Traditional Süssmayr completion of Mozart’s Lacrimosa; performing edition and Walter’s alterations unidentified.
fields.note: Mozart’s surviving draft breaks off after bar 8. The conventional completion continues the movement and closes with the short Amen, rather than a later reconstructed Amen fugue. The NMA distinguishes Eybler’s separate attempted continuation from Süssmayr’s completed version. The upload does not identify its performing edition; no second-by-second authorship seam or session-specific trombone cut list is claimed.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The primary concert archive identifies Thursday 26 July 1956; Commons, Internet Archive and the discography agree. This is the live performance date, not the date of first publication, a later commercial issue, digitisation or upload.

fields.value: Rule 1 — territorial recording claim: Commons applies PD-EU-audio; upstream Internet Archive applies Public Domain Mark 1.0.
fields.note: The documented fact is the sources’ sound-recording rights assertion. PD-EU-audio is territorial: US status is not established, and no worldwide clearance is claimed. Public Domain Mark is not CC0 or a performer’s licence. The 1956 performance date does not prove first lawful publication or communication before 1963; that history is unestablished. The known 1996 Orfeo issue and 2018 uploads are not substituted for it. Admission therefore uses the explicit Commons PD-EU-audio route, not a calculated pre-1963-publication claim.

facts: By his father Leopold; extensive performing tours from childhood
Salzburg · Italy · Mannheim and Paris · Vienna from 1781

composer.background:
Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756, the seventh child of Leopold Mozart and Anna Maria Pertl; only he and his sister Maria Anna survived infancy. Leopold was a violinist and composer in the archbishop’s service, and in the year of Wolfgang’s birth published an influential violin treatise. He taught both children. Maria Anna, called Nannerl within the family, became an accomplished keyboard player, and the first tours presented brother and sister together. The family’s travels were an educational system as well as a business: the children encountered instruments, performers, repertories and audiences that a Salzburg childhood alone could not have supplied.

The long tour of 1763–66 took them through German courts, Paris, London and the Netherlands. In London Mozart met Johann Christian Bach, whose clear phrases and Italianate melodic style offered a model different from the contrapuntal teaching associated with Bach’s father. Illness repeatedly interrupted the itinerary. Leopold managed engagements, publicity and money while supervising composition, and the surviving correspondence documents the costs and uncertainties behind the public demonstrations. Wolfgang learned to write for named performers and immediate occasions before he had an independent adult household.
